thyme.region_notes_beginner: Thyme is easy across the maritime Pacific Northwest. It is hardy well beyond both zones here, and the region's mild, dry summer suits this low, spreading herb well. Plant in spring a few weeks after your last frost, give it full sun and fast-draining soil, and it flowers in summer, a little later on the cooler coast than inland.
thyme.region_notes_seasoned: Thyme is a hardy, trouble-free, low spreading perennial across both maritime Pacific Northwest zones: common thyme is reliably hardy to about zone 5 (NCSU 5a to 9b; PSU/UF z5-9), well beyond either zone 8 or 9 here, and the region's mild, dry summer suits this Mediterranean sub-shrub without the humidity stress it faces further south and east. Set plants out a few weeks after the last spring frost, in full sun with lean, sharply drained soil. Bloom runs from late May in the warmer inland zone (8) to about a week later on the cooler, later-warming immediate coast (9); resolve each zone's window from its own frost dates rather than assuming the milder-numbered coastal zone runs earlier. Do the shaping shear after bloom fades, not in late fall.

blueberry.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
blueberry.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). Northern highbush is the recommended_type in both zones, matching WSU's own framing of northern highbush as the common Washington type and the ample WSU Skagit-station-sourced winter chill (968 to 1,950 hours z8, 700 to 1,500 hours z9, region_chill_delivered.pnw) against this crop's 1,000 hour requirement. Plant/bloom/harvest windows sourced to WSU Skagit County Extension, 'Growing Blueberries: Start With the Right Soil' (Ranten 2025, citing WSU NWREC small-fruit horticulturist Lisa Wasko DeVetter): plant January-March (dormant), net against birds mid-June through harvest completion in August, prune in winter or early spring. Bloom month (April) is a reasoned placement (the source states pre-bloom dormant pruning and dormant planting windows but no explicit bloom date; April is the standard maritime-PNW Vaccinium bloom window and clears both zones' last frost with margin). Both zones share one window; the source is a general western-WA guide, not zone-differentiated. resolution_method is frost_anchored_resolved per the pnw cell contract's frost-anchored invariant (not berries_woody_precompute, which other regions use); resolved_from carries the real NOAA-normal frost dates per zone.

8.type_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is the blueberry to plant here. West of the Cascades, winters bank about 968 to 1,950 hours (average around 1,468) of winter chill, WSU Skagit County Extension station data, comfortably clearing this crop's roughly 1,000 hour chill requirement. The other real requirement is soil: native soils west of the Cascades are rarely acidic enough on their own, so start right by testing and amending to pH 4.5 to 5.5, or grow in containers or raised beds with an acidic mix (WSU).
8.type_note_beginner: Plant northern highbush blueberries here. Our winters are plenty cold for this type. The bigger job is the soil: it needs to be quite acidic, more than most of our native soil, so test it and add sulfur or peat, or just grow your bushes in a large pot or raised bed with an acidic potting mix.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in April is comfortably behind the typical last frost here
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Blueberry is a permanent deciduous shrub here, planted once and productive for decades. It rests bare and dormant through the mild, wet winter, then breaks bud and blooms in April, sets fruit through a long cool spring, and ripens from late June into August. Net the bushes against birds from mid-June through the end of harvest, and prune in the dormant season, winter into early spring, just before growth resumes. Plant at least two cultivars near each other for the best fruit set.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blueberry bush comes back every year and can produce for decades. It drops its leaves and rests over our mild winter, flowers in April, and ripens fruit from late June through August. Net the bushes starting in mid-June, before the birds beat you to the berries, and prune in winter or very early spring. Plant two different varieties together for a bigger crop.

blueberry.region_notes_beginner: The maritime Northwest, from Puget Sound into the Willamette Valley, is premier blueberry country: our winters deliver plenty of the cold rest this bush needs, and northern highbush is the variety type to grow. Plant dormant bushes January through March, expect flowers in April, and pick fruit from late June into August. The one thing our soil does not give this plant for free is acidity, so amend your soil or grow in a large pot or raised bed with an acidic mix, and plant two varieties for a bigger harvest.
blueberry.region_notes_seasoned: West of the Cascades is a premier blueberry region: WSU Skagit County station data shows winters banking roughly 968 to 1,950 chill hours (zone 8) and 700 to 1,500 (zone 9), comfortably clearing northern highbush's requirement in the great majority of winters. Set dormant plants January through March, expect bloom in April, and net against birds from mid-June through the close of harvest in August. Acidic soil, not chill, is the limiting factor here: test and amend to pH 4.5 to 5.5, or grow in containers or raised beds with an acidic mix, since native soils west of the Cascades rarely arrive acidic enough on their own. Plant at least two cultivars for the best fruit set.

raspberry.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
raspberry.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). recommended_type summer_bearing in both zones: Washington's commercial red raspberry industry (the nation's largest, per USDA NASS) is built on summer-bearing (Meeker-type) cultivars in this exact maritime climate, a confident, sourced strength claim, not a hedge. Harvest window (June-August, with a second fall flush on everbearing types into September) is T1-sourced to WSU Extension's Whatcom County 'Seasonal Harvest Guide'. WSU's dedicated caneberry cultural bulletin (EM103E) has no freely available .edu-hosted copy located this pass (flash-drive only per WSU's own catalog), so plant_out/bloom timing is treated conservatively: dormant bare-root planting in the standard late-fall-through-winter window, bloom in May (about one month ahead of the June harvest start, the standard cane-fruit bloom-to-harvest interval already used for this crop's other certified regions), not claimed as independently WSU-PNW-sourced. Both zones share one window (the source is not zone-differentiated); resolved_from carries the real per-zone NOAA frost normals.

8.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) red raspberry is the type to plant here, and it is not a modest claim: Washington is the number one red raspberry producing state in the country, almost all of it summer-bearing cultivars (Meeker and its kin) grown in this same maritime climate. Chill is never the limiter (this crop needs about 800 hours and the region banks 968 to 1,950), so the choice comes down to cultivar and trellising, not survival.
8.type_note_beginner: Plant a summer-bearing red raspberry, the classic type. This is genuinely raspberry country: Washington grows more red raspberries than any other state, and our winters give this plant all the cold rest it needs.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Raspberries bloom in May, well after this zone's typical late-March last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk here
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit here as everywhere: the canes drop their leaves and rest through the mild, wet winter, banking the modest chill the plant needs. The perennial crown lives for a decade or more while each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes from late fall through winter, train them on a trellis, and prune out the spent fruited canes and thin the new ones in the dormant season.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch comes back every year, even though each individual cane only lives two seasons: it grows one year, then fruits and dies the next, while fresh canes keep coming up from the roots. Plant dormant canes in late fall or winter, give them a trellis, and cut out the canes that already fruited each winter.

raspberry.region_notes_seasoned: West of the Cascades is the heart of the US red raspberry industry, and Washington is the number one red raspberry state in the country, grown almost entirely as summer-bearing (floricane) cultivars in this exact climate. Set dormant bare-root canes from late fall through winter, trellis them, and expect bloom in May and a heavy harvest from June into August; everbearing types add a second flush into September. Chill (about 800 hours needed, far more banked here) is never the limiting factor; cultivar choice and trellising are what separate a good patch from a great one.

blackberry.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
blackberry.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). recommended_type summer_bearing in both zones (trailing marionberry/boysenberry/loganberry plus upright thornless types are all floricane/summer-bearing). Harvest window (July-August, matching Blackberry and Boysenberry/Marionberry/Loganberry/Tayberry alike) is T1-sourced to WSU Extension's Whatcom County 'Seasonal Harvest Guide'. As with raspberry, WSU's dedicated caneberry cultural bulletin (EM103E) has no free .edu-hosted copy located this pass, so plant_out/bloom timing is treated conservatively (standard dormant bare-root window; bloom about one month ahead of the July harvest start, the same cane-fruit interval convention used elsewhere for this crop). No WSU source located this pass frames an invasive-Himalayan-blackberry caveat for the home-garden planting guidance used here, so none is asserted. Both zones share one window; resolved_from carries the real per-zone NOAA frost normals.

8.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) blackberry is the type to plant here, and this is the crop's home ground: marionberry, the trailing blackberry cultivar behind most commercial Pacific Northwest blackberry production, was bred in Oregon and remains an Oregon-bred signature of this exact climate. Trailing types (marionberry, boysenberry, loganberry) need a trellis for their long canes; upright thornless types are a lower-maintenance alternative. Chill (about 400 hours needed) is never a limiter here.
8.type_note_beginner: Plant a summer-bearing blackberry. If you want the famous local flavor, look for marionberry, a trailing type bred right here in Oregon; it needs a trellis for its long canes. Upright thornless types are easier to manage if you would rather skip the trellis work.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blackberries bloom in May, well after this zone's typical late-March last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk here
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Blackberry is a deciduous cane fruit here: the canes drop their leaves and rest through the mild, wet winter, while the perennial crown and roots live for 15 to 20 years and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes from late fall through winter, trellis the trailing types (their long canes root wherever they touch ground if left untrellised), and prune out the spent fruited canes each dormant season.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blackberry patch is permanent, even though each cane only lives two years: it grows one season, fruits the next, then dies while new canes take over. Plant dormant canes in late fall or winter, put trailing types like marionberry on a trellis, and cut out the old fruited canes each winter.

blackberry.region_notes_seasoned: The maritime Northwest is blackberry country, and marionberry, an Oregon-bred trailing cultivar, remains the region's signature: it and its trailing relatives (boysenberry, loganberry) deliver intense flavor here and need a two-wire trellis for their long canes. Upright and semi-erect thornless types grow well too, with less training work. Set dormant bare-root canes from late fall through winter, expect bloom in May and harvest from July into August, and prune out spent fruited canes each dormant season. Chill (about 400 hours needed) is never a limiting factor here.

elderberry.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
elderberry.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). No WSU/OSU PNW-specific elderberry cultural-timing source was located this pass (WSU's tree-fruit handbook, EB0937, explicitly does not cover elderberry, and no dedicated WSU/OSU elderberry bulletin was found -- a fully thin gap for this region specifically, flagged in the T1 sourcing table). This cell instead applies the same general, cross-region American elderberry biology already carried by this crop's other certified regions (mu_ext, Missouri Extension AF1017; msu_ext, Michigan State Extension), reconciled to the pnw frost dates: one recommended_type everywhere, chosen by cultivar not climate, roughly 400 chill hours needed (trivial against this region's banked chill), June bloom, August-September ripening, matching the window this crop already carries in its existing ca_north_coast cell (a comparably mild, wet-winter maritime climate). Framed honestly as adaptable-elsewhere guidance applied here, not a PNW-specific finding; the region's genuine strength for this crop is its ample rainfall and moisture, which elderberry, unlike most other fruiting shrubs in this dataset, actually prefers. Both zones share one window; resolved_from carries the real per-zone NOAA frost normals.

8.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the one type to grow, chosen by cultivar rather than by climate, and the maritime Northwest suits it well: this is a moisture-loving shrub, and our long wet season and mild winters are close to ideal. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and needs only about 400 chill hours, far less than this region banks, so chill is never a concern. Plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
8.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, the one common type. It loves moisture, so our wet climate is genuinely a plus for this plant, and our winters are more than cold enough for it. Plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in June, well after the last frost in either zone, so frost on bloom is not a concern here.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent, very cold-hardy deciduous shrub here, planted once and renewed in place for many years. It rests dormant through the mild, wet winter, leafs out and grows fast in spring, blooms in June, and ripens clusters of dark berries from August into September. Renew the oldest canes in late winter and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set; this native, adaptable shrub asks for little beyond the moisture this region already supplies.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived, very cold-hardy bush you plant once and keep for years. It rests over our mild winter, grows fast in spring, flowers in June, and ripens dark berries from August into September. Prune the oldest stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties for a bigger crop; our wet climate actually suits this plant well.

strawberry.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked; the crowns are dormant stock, so there is no need to wait out frost danger (WSU Clallam County Extension).

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: June-bearing plants on an established bed flower in May here, roughly a month ahead of the June harvest start; open blossoms are damaged at 30°F (WSU Clallam County Extension).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: June-bearing strawberries crop June-July here, the type-defining window (WSU Clallam County Extension).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The June-bearing flush runs into July. Renovate the matted row within about a week of the last picking: mow the leaves, narrow the row, and fertilize (WSU Clallam County Extension).

strawberry.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). grown_as=perennial (June-bearing matted-row), matching WSU Clallam County Extension's 'Growing Strawberries' (Stehr-Green 2021): June-bearers crop June-July, the recommended maritime cultivars are Benton, Hood, Rainier, Puget Reliance, Puget Summer, Sweet Sunrise, Shuksan, and Tillamook, winter hardiness to the crown runs 10 to 20°F but open blossoms are damaged at 30°F, and beds are renovated about a week after the last picking. bloom/harvest are taken directly from the source's stated absolute calendar (June-July is the type's own name), not mechanically derived by transplanting this crop's northern_tier last-frost-offset formula onto pnw's much earlier last-frost date (that formula, tuned for zones with a May last frost, would place bloom/harvest in April/May here, contradicting the source's own June-bearing framing) -- plant_out alone keeps the frost-offset rule (dormant bare-root timing genuinely is frost/soil-workability driven and transfers region to region), giving Mar 7-28 (z8) and Mar 15-Apr 5 (z9). Zone 8 sits at the crown-hardiness edge (USDA zone 8 winter low 10-20°F versus the source's 10-20°F crown-hardiness floor); zone 9 (winter low 20-30°F) sits comfortably above it -- an honest, zone-specific distinction carried into grown_as_note_seasoned/beginner. Both zones otherwise share one window (the source is a general western-WA guide); resolved_from carries the real per-zone NOAA frost normals.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: West of the Cascades, strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, the same dominant US backyard system used farther north, and June-bearing types are the real signature here: WSU Clallam County Extension names Benton, Hood, Rainier, Puget Reliance, Puget Summer, Sweet Sunrise, Shuksan, and Tillamook as the recommended maritime cultivars. Set dormant bare-root crowns as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, about two weeks before the last frost. Renovate the bed within about a week of the last picking: mow the foliage, narrow the row, and fertilize. Zone 8 sits right at this crop's cold edge for the crown (hardy to 10 to 20°F, and this zone's own USDA winter-low band runs the same 10 to 20°F), so mulch with straw after the ground first freezes and pull it back as growth resumes in spring.
